# Summary of Education in Finland
Education in Finland has deep historical roots tied to Lutheranism, emphasizing literacy for reading the Bible. The first Finnish university was founded in 1640, and literacy rates rose significantly by the 19th century. A basic school system evolved over time—initially divided between primary kansakoulu and the more selective oppikoulu—and schooling became mandatory in 1921. The modern compulsory education system mandates nine years of comprehensive schooling for children aged 7 to 16 (expanded to upper secondary education by 2021), after which students may choose between academic (lukio) or vocational tracks. Finnish municipalities administer most schools, which emphasize small classes, educational equity, minimal homework, student well-being, and strong social support such as free meals, books, and health care.
Early childhood education is highly valued, with universal access to free daycare and a focus on developing social skills, independence, and lifelong learning through play until formal schooling begins at age seven. Teacher education is rigorous, requiring a master's degree for both primary and secondary educators, reflecting the profession’s high respect. Tertiary education comprises traditional universities offering research-based education and universities of applied sciences emphasizing practical skills, with admissions based on transparent, meritocratic exams. Tuition is free for EU/EEA students, while non-European students pay fees. Finland’s education system promotes multilingualism, with students typically learning Finnish or Swedish plus at least two additional languages. Ongoing reforms include integrating phenomenon-based learning to foster 21st-century skills. Finland also exports its educational model internationally through official Finnish curriculum schools and Finnish-inspired private schools worldwide, supported by coordinated national programs.
